newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's ruling Islamists pass censure test.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's ruling Islamists pass censure test.

text.p: Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan hung on to power on Tuesday, narrowly surviving an opposition attempt to oust his coalition government for its Islamist leanings.
Deputies voted 271 against 265 to drop an opposition censure motion, which criticises the government for straying from the country's decades-old secularist path.
"The government will carry out its duties until the year 2000 and give Turkey a respected place in the world," Erbakan told a news conference after the vote.
It was the slimmest margin in three censure motions Erbakan has won since he became modern Turkey's first Islamist leader last June.
The coalition has been embroiled in recent months in a row with the powerful, secularist military -- which is strongly backed by the mainstream media -- over Islamist activism.
Despite the victory Erbakan faces an uncertain future, with dissident government MPs trying to craft an Islamist-free coalition formula with the fractious opposition.

A former cabinet member has held extensive talks with the opposition to set up a secularist alliance and a deputy from Erbakan's Welfare Party defected to the opposition on Monday in an unprecedented break in the Islamists' solidarity.
Three ministers from the government's conservative True Path Party wing have quit in the last month, citing unease at Erbakan's bid to increase the role of religion in public life.
Main opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz accused Erbakan of upsetting the social balances of Moslem-but-secular Turkey with plans for mild Islamist reforms.

"Is it not the case that (the government) has created a very dangerous tension and polarisation between believers and non-believers, secularists and anti-secularists?" Motherland Party leader Yilmaz asked parliament.
The army, which has carried out three coups since 1960, says its fight against Islamism is a matter of "life or death".
Istanbul's stock exchange, highly sensitive to political developments, closed 1.21 percent up ahead of the vote.
Brokers say the market is hopeful that secularists can form an alternative government and ditch Erbakan without going to elections.
The instability has disrupted the government's plans to reverse a huge budget deficit with the help of $4.5 billion in privatisation revenues.
The next test for Erbakan is likely to be a meeting of the military-dominated National Security Council at the end of May.
The monthly council meetings have turned into regular showdowns between Erbakan and the generals, who have pressured him to carry out a list of 18 anti-Islamist demands.
The parliamentary speaker adjourned Tuesday's debate for 10 minutes when opposition MPs and deputies from Erbakan's Welfare Party brawled with each other.
MPs began to rush to the front after Yilmaz referred to a statement by the army that accused the government of hostility towards Kemal Ataturk, Turkey's revered secularist founder.
"The general staff said 'We cannot be in harmony with the enemies of Ataturk'," Yilmaz said.
He also repeated newspaper accusations that the army did not tell the government in advance about a current anti-rebel military drive into northern Iraq involving thousands of Turkish troops.
